title: Har Rai and Har Krishan
hook: remember Guru Har Rai, and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes

segments.voice: Yesterday: miri piri, and your line: arjan, hargobind. Today the Ardas names the seventh Guru, and the eighth, who was a child.

In the middle of New Delhi, a short walk from the government buildings, there's a white gurdwara with a golden dome and a large pool of water. Every day, people carry the water home in bottles: for a sick parent, for a child with a fever, for themselves. Ask why, and you'll hear about a boy. Tradition says a deadly epidemic, remembered as smallpox, was moving through Delhi, and a Guru who was still a child stayed in the city and went among the sick. That place is Gurdwara Bangla Sahib, and the boy is remembered every time the Ardas is said.
screen: `A WHITE GURDWARA IN NEW DELHI.` → `WATER CARRIED HOME IN BOTTLES.` → `A GURU WHO WAS A CHILD.`

segments.voice: The Ardas line runs on: sri harirai, remember the revered Har Rai. Then: sri harkrishan dhiaaeeai, jis ditthai sabh dukh jaai. Meditate on Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes. Guru Har Rai, the seventh Guru, was the grandson of Guru Hargobind. He is remembered for his gentleness. Tradition says he kept a garden and a dispensary of herbal medicines at Kiratpur, open to anyone who needed them, and a well-known story says that once, when his robe brushed a flower and broke it, he was saddened, and spoke about how easily we damage what we can't mend. His son, Har Krishan, became Guru while still a small child. He was called to Delhi, and while he was there, the epidemic broke out. Tradition says he tended the sick in the city, and that he caught the disease himself and died there, still a child. Gurdwara Bangla Sahib stands where he stayed. Look at what the Ardas says. It doesn't call him small, or young, or tragic. It says: seeing him, all pain goes. Dukh, the Punjabi word for pain and sorrow, simply leaves. People who have sat with a sick relative sometimes describe what happens when a small child walks into the room: the air changes. The Ardas sets that ordinary experience at the heart of the prayer: a child's calm face, and the pain going out of a room. A gentle father, then his child, a Guru who stayed when it was dangerous.
screen: `HAR RAI: THE GENTLE GURU.` · `A GARDEN, AND A BROKEN FLOWER.` · `HAR KRISHAN STAYED IN DELHI.` · `SEEING HIM, ALL PAIN GOES.` · then, large: `ALL PAIN GOES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a child you know, or once knew, or once were, at a quiet moment, asleep or absorbed in a game, and let their face stay in front of you. Let some of today's tension go out on the breath, the way it goes out of a room when a child walks in. If you pray, say Waheguru, or the Ardas's own words, sabh dukh jaai, all pain goes.
Dukh, pain or sorrow. Seeing Guru Har Krishan, the child Guru who stayed among the sick, all dukh goes.
Your line: all pain goes. A child who stayed when it was dangerous. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Har Rai and Guru Har Krishan, seeing whom all pain goes; pilgrims visit Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi and take water from its sarovar for the sick.

chat.says: Why do people take water home from Bangla Sahib in Delhi?
options: To remember the child Guru who stayed among the sick: seeing him, all pain goes.
The water was brought there from a holy river by Guru Har Rai himself.
It's a custom from long before the Gurus, older than the city itself.
chat.meaning: Tradition says Guru Har Krishan tended Delhi's sick and died there, still a child. The Ardas says: seeing him, all dukh goes.
